title: Genotype, Phenotype, and Phenotypic Plasticity
objective: Separate inherited genotype from the phenotype expressed at a particular stage, place, treatment, and sampling method.

terms.definition: An individual's inherited DNA sequence state, either genome-wide or at specified loci.
An observed or measured characteristic produced by biology under defined conditions.
Capacity of one genotype to express different phenotypes across environments or development.
Pattern of a genotype's phenotype across an environmental gradient or set of environments.

coreScience: Phenotype is not genotype made visible without interference. A useful model is phenotype = genotype + environment + genotype-by-environment interaction + development + measurement error. Plant age, node position, reproductive status, canopy location, root condition, and prior stress can change the measured outcome.

Plasticity can be adaptive, neutral, or harmful. The same clone may change branch number under different spectra, rooting success under different propagation environments, or metabolite concentration across canopy positions and harvest dates. Such changes do not automatically indicate genetic contamination.

A phenotype becomes comparable only after the protocol defines the organ, stage, environment, unit, sampling intensity, and data treatment. Photographs are valuable records but rarely replace quantitative measurements or chemistry.
cultivationRelevance: Use clones as paired environmental tests only when identity and health are confirmed and the ramets are randomized. Otherwise source-plant position, cutting size, or pathogen status can masquerade as treatment plasticity.
Preserve unusual phenotypes for retest before naming a new line. A stable genetic difference should repeat under common conditions or be supported by identity testing.

measureAndRecord.requirement: Clone or seed-family ID, source, generation, markers if used, and custody.
Trait, organ, stage, position, unit, instrument, and scoring threshold.
Light, photoperiod, air and root-zone conditions, nutrition, water, density, and stress.
Age, node count, floral stage, days from transition, and prior treatment.
Replicates, randomization, control genotype, second run, and outcome consistency.

misconceptions: Clones should look identical: Shared genotype does not erase environmental, developmental, or biological variation.
Any off-type is a mutation: Mislabeling, plasticity, disease, nutrition, and sampling should be tested first.
A memorable phenotype is stable: Stability requires repeated expression and an explicit test environment.
evidenceLimits: Cannabis plasticity studies cover limited genotypes and traits. Common-environment retesting can separate some causes, but it does not prove the molecular mechanism.
